title: Why Nico Williams' Extra-Time Goal Was Disallowed in the World Cup Final
excerpt: The referee ruled Mikel Merino fouled Nicolás Otamendi before Williams scored, but the call could not be reviewed by VAR because the whistle came before the ball crossed the line.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Nico Williams' goal in the World Cup final was disallowed due to a foul by Mikel Merino.
  • VAR could not review the decision because the referee's whistle blew before the goal was scored.
  • Mark Halsey criticized the foul call, stating it should have been a goal for Spain.
  • Spain won the match 1-0, but the disallowed goal remains a controversial topic.
  • The incident raises questions about VAR's effectiveness in critical moments of the game.
The Disallowed Goal Controversy
›Nico Williams scored in the 96th minute.
›Referee Slavko Vinčić ruled a foul by Mikel Merino.
›VAR could not intervene due to the early whistle.
›Mark Halsey argued it should have been a goal.
  • Nico Williams' apparent go-ahead goal in the 96th minute of the World Cup final was disallowed after referee Slavko Vinčić ruled that Mikel Merino fouled Nicolás Otamendi in the build-up.
  • Replays showed Merino's left foot stepping on Otamendi's left foot, but ex-Premier League referee Mark Halsey said VAR should have intervened and the goal should have stood.
  • The decision was not reviewable by VAR because Vinčić had blown his whistle before Williams scored, meaning the goal was already ruled out before the ball hit the net.
  • Spain eventually won 1-0 through Ferran Torres' 106th-minute strike, but the disallowed goal remains the most debated moment of the 2026 World Cup.

The Disallowed Goal

With the World Cup final scoreless in extra time and Argentina down to 10 men following Enzo Fernández's red card, Spain appeared to break through in the 96th minute. Dani Olmo and Mikel Merino combined to work the ball into the box, where Nico Williams met it and slotted past Emiliano Martínez.

The Athletic Bilbao winger wheeled away in celebration — then stopped. Referee Slavko Vinčić had blown his whistle before Williams scored, ruling that Merino had fouled Argentina defender Nicolás Otamendi in the build-up. Replays showed Merino's left foot stepping on top of Otamendi's left foot as the pair jostled for position. Otamendi went down clutching his leg.

""I'm sorry, that's not a foul for me," he told The Sun."

What made the decision particularly contentious was its procedural finality. CBS Sports analyst Nico Cantor explained that because Vinčić had whistled before the ball crossed the line, the goal was never formally scored — meaning VAR could not intervene to recommend a review. Had Vinčić waited and allowed play to continue, the Video Assistant Referee could have checked whether the foul was correct.

Referees Divided on the Call

Former Premier League referee Mark Halsey was blunt in his assessment. "I'm sorry, that's not a foul for me," he told The Sun. "He's bought that with the way he's thrown himself up in the air and the referee's given a free-kick. Why on earth doesn't VAR look at that, check it properly and recommend a review? For me, that's no foul, and it should have been a goal for Spain."

"Why on earth doesn't VAR look at that, check it properly and recommend a review? For me, that's no foul, and it should have been a goal for Spain."

— Mark Halsey, former Premier League referee

The call appeared particularly harsh given the context. Otamendi, the 38-year-old former Manchester City defender, appeared to exaggerate the contact — a common defensive tactic but one that referees are increasingly expected to see through. The question of whether Merino's contact was enough to constitute a foul, or whether Otamendi sold it, will likely be debated for years.

Spain Won Anyway — But the Debate Endures

Spain did not let the setback derail them. Ten minutes after the disallowed goal, Ferran Torres smashed home from close range in the 106th minute after Williams headed a Pedro Porro cross back across goal. Torres raced to the corner flag, echoing Andrés Iniesta's celebration after Spain's 2010 World Cup-winning goal in Johannesburg.

"In the end, the goal belongs to 47 million people. Not me, nor we 26 players here. Destiny was written today. We were going to win."

— Ferran Torres, Spain forward
Spain's Victory Amidst Debate
›Ferran Torres scored the winning goal in the 106th minute.
›Spain won the match 1-0 against Argentina.
›Williams was a key player despite the disallowed goal.
›The disallowed goal remains a hot topic of discussion.

Williams himself had come close multiple times before Torres' winner. He was denied by a strong Martínez save from a header earlier in extra time, and had also created the chance that led to the winning goal. Despite missing out on the scoresheet, the 24-year-old was one of Spain's most dangerous players throughout the tournament.

VAR's Limits Exposed Again

The incident highlights an ongoing debate about VAR's role in football's biggest moments. The technology was introduced to correct "clear and obvious errors," but its ability to do so depends entirely on the match referee's initial decision and timing. When a referee blows early — as Vinčić did here — VAR is powerless. FIFA will face questions about whether the protocol needs to change so that officials allow play to continue in borderline situations, letting VAR serve as the safety net it was designed to be.
